SUPPLEMENTARYMATERIAL
Additional Experiments
Frontier Transfer.We explore whether configurations that perform well on one task remain effective on other tasks. For
each source task, we construct its task-specific Pareto frontier using 200 policy rollouts from a diffusion policy trained
exclusively on that task. We then apply the configurations on this frontier to each of the other three tasks and retain the
Pareto-optimal points to form a transferred frontier.
To measure how closely each transferred frontier matches the target task’s native frontier, we compute the hypervolume
ratio (HVR). Specifically, we divide the area under the transferred frontier by the area under the native frontier. The trigger-
time range extends from zero to the latest non-dominated point reached by either frontier. An HVR near one indicates that
the transferred configurations retain most of the accuracy–latency tradeoff obtained by task-specific tuning.
The results for each source-target task pair are shown in Figure6. Across the 12 ordered source-target pairs, Reward-
DAgger achieves a mean HVR of0.92and a median HVR of0.93, indicating thathigh-performing regions of the gate
configuration space are largely shared across tasks.
